uncited: **Inputs:** A set of $N$ points in an $n$-dimensional feature space.
Each point represents a voxel's multi-variate data values.
**Outputs:** A hierarchical cluster tree and an assignment of a unique cluster ID and density value to each input point.
**Histogram:** An $n$-dimensional grid of cells.
Each cell stores a count of points falling within its bounds.
**Cluster Tree:** A tree structure where nodes represent clusters.
Each node contains a list of point indices belonging to that cluster (excluding those in child clusters).
**Point Attributes:** Each point stores its assigned `cluster_id` and `density`.
*   Cell Size: The pre-defined size for the $n$-dimensional histogram bins.
This parameter determines the resolution of the density estimation.
Build an $n$-dimensional histogram with the specified cell size.
For each point $p$ in the input set, determine which histogram cell $c$ it falls into.
The density estimate for any point in cell $c$ is equal to the count of points in that cell.
Create a root cluster $C_{root}$ with density 0.
Initialize $C_{root}$ to contain all $N$ input points.
Identify all connected components in the histogram where cells have density $\ge 1$.
Two cells are connected if they share a face, edge, or vertex (i.e., they are 26-connected in 3D, or generally $3^n-1$ connected in $n$-dimensions).
Each connected component forms a cluster of density 1.
Add these clusters as children of the root.
Let $D_{max}$ be the maximum density value present in the histogram.
Identify all cells with density exactly equal to $d$.
Remove these cells from the active histogram (conceptually, they are no longer part of the connected components for higher densities).
Check the connected components formed by cells with density $> d$.

If a previously existing cluster (connected component at density $d$) splits into $k > 1$ new connected components due to the removal of cells at density $d$, create $k$ new child clusters for the parent cluster.
These new clusters correspond to the new connected components.
Assign a unique cluster ID to each new cluster.
The process stops when the maximum density $D_{max}$ is reached.
Clusters at the highest density level are leaf nodes.
For each cluster, assign its unique ID to all points contained within it.
However, points contained in any child cluster overwrite the ID assigned by the parent.
Consequently, each inner node contains all points of the cluster that are *not* contained in any sub-cluster.
The root node contains all points not part of any other cluster.
If too small, noise creates spurious clusters.
*   **Boundaries:** Points on the boundary of the feature space may have artificially low densities if the histogram is not padded or handled correctly.
*   **Degenerate Input:** If all points have the same density, only one cluster (the root) or a single level of clusters will exist.
*   **Connectivity Definition:** The definition of "connected" (face, edge, vertex) must be consistent with the dimensionality $n$.
In high dimensions, the number of neighbors grows exponentially ($3^n - 1$).
*   **Time Complexity:** Building the histogram is $O(N)$.
Finding connected components depends on the number of cells and their connectivity.
In the worst case, it can be expensive in high dimensions due to the exponential growth of neighbors.
